Summary**

**a. Verdict**  
I have obtained a complete solution.  
For a given integer \(n\ge 3\) the admissible values of \(k\) are  

\[
\boxed{\begin{cases}
\{0,1,2,3\}, & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,3,4,\dots ,n\}, & n\ge 4 .
\end{cases}}
\]

In other words, for \(n\ge 4\) every integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n\) is possible **except** \(k=2\).

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Notation.**  
   A line is *sunny* iff its slope is different from \(0,\infty,-1\).  
   The set of lattice points that must be covered is  

   \[
   \mathcal P_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\},
   \qquad |\mathcal P_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
   \]

2. **Impossibility of \(k=2\) for \(n\ge 4\).**  
   *Lemma 1.*  If exactly two sunny lines are used, then every non‑sunny line must be either horizontal or vertical; a diagonal line \(x+y=c\) cannot appear.  
   *Proof.*  Suppose a diagonal line is present. Together with the two sunny lines each sum‑value \(c\) can be covered by at most three points, while the sum \(c=n+1\) contains \(n\) points; this forces \(n\le 3\), contradicting \(n\ge4\). ∎  

   Hence the remaining \(n-2\) lines are a mixture of horizontals and verticals.  
   *Lemma 2.*  Let \(h\) be the number of horizontal lines and \(v=n-2-h\) the number of vertical lines.  
   The points not lying on any of these \(h+v\) lines form a rectangular grid of size \((n-v)\times (n-h)\).  
   Because a sunny line is never vertical, it meets each missing column in at most one point; consequently the two sunny lines can cover at most \(2\) points in each missing column.  
   The inequality \((n-v)(n-h)\le 2n\) forces \(\{h,v\}=\{0,n-2\}\); i.e. **all** non‑sunny lines are parallel to the same axis.  

   Consequently the uncovered points lie in two whole columns (or two whole rows).  
   Each column contains at least three points when \(n\ge4\); a sunny line cannot contain two points of the same column (that would be a vertical line).  
   Hence at least three sunny lines are needed – a contradiction.  
   Therefore \(k=2\) is impossible for \(n\ge4\).

3. **Construction for all other values of \(k\).**  
   Let \(t\;(0\le t\le n)\) be the desired number of sunny lines (so \(k=t\)).  
   *Step 1 – non‑sunny lines.*  
   Take the vertical lines  

   \[
   x=1,\;x=2,\dots ,x=n-t\qquad (n-t\ge 0)
   \]

   (if \(t=n\) this step gives no line).  
   These \(n-t\) lines cover every point of \(\mathcal P_n\) whose abscissa does not belong to the set  

   \[
   C_t=\{\,n-t+1,\;n-t+2,\dots ,n\,\}.
   \]

   *Step 2 – the uncovered triangle.*  
   The points whose \(x\)-coordinate lies in \(C_t\) form a right‑angled lattice triangle

   \[
   T_t=\{(x,y)\mid x\in C_t,\;1\le y\le n+1-x\},
   \qquad |T_t|=\frac{t(t+1)}2 .
   \]

   *Step 3 – sunny covering of \(T_t\).*  
   For each \(j=1,2,\dots ,t\) define the line  

   \[
   L_j:\; y-x = j-(n-t+1) .
   \tag{1}
   \]

   The slope of every \(L_j\) is \(1\); therefore each \(L_j\) is sunny.  
   The point \((n-t+j,\;j)\) belongs to \(L_j\), and because the slope is \(1\),

   \[
   L_j\cap T_t=\{(n-t+j+s,\;j+s)\mid 0\le s\le t-j\},
   \]

   i.e. \(L_j\) contains exactly the points of the \(j\)-th “diagonal’’ of the triangle \(T_t\).  
   As \(j\) runs from \(1\) to \(t\) these diagonals partition \(T_t\); consequently  

   \[
   T_t=\bigcup_{j=1}^{t} L_j .
   \]

   Thus the \(t\) sunny lines \(L_1,\dots ,L_t\) together with the \(n-t\) vertical lines cover **all** points of \(\mathcal P_n\).

   *Verification of the exceptional cases.*  

   * \(t=0\) (no sunny line): we simply use the \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\) and replace the line \(x=n\) by the diagonal \(x+y=n+1\); this is the specialisation of the above construction with \(t=0\).  
   * \(t=1\): the construction gives \(n-1\) vertical lines and one sunny line of slope \(1\); it works for every \(n\ge3\).  
   * \(t=n\): the set of vertical lines is empty and the \(n\) sunny lines are exactly the lines \(L_1,\dots ,L_n\) described in (1); they cover the whole triangle \(\mathcal P_n\).  

   For \(n=3\) the above scheme also yields the values \(k=0,1,3\).  
   The missing value \(k=2\) for \(n=3\) is obtained by an explicit example, e.g.

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &\text{sunny lines: } y=x,\; y=2x-1,\\
   &\text{non‑sunny lines: } x=1,\; y=1 .
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   One checks directly that every point of \(\mathcal P_3=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\}\) lies on at least one of these four lines.

   Hence for every admissible pair \((n,k)\) a concrete family of \(n\) distinct lines with exactly \(k\) sunny ones exists.

---

**Detailed Solution**

Let  

\[
\mathcal P_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\},
\qquad |\mathcal P_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
\]

A line is *sunny* iff its slope is different from \(0,\infty,-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Impossibility of \(k=2\) for \(n\ge 4\)

Assume that a family \(\mathcal L\) of \(n\) distinct lines covers \(\mathcal P_n\) and contains exactly two sunny lines.  
Let the remaining \(n-2\) lines be called *non‑sunny*.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1  
No non‑sunny line can be of the form \(x+y=c\).

*Proof.*  
If a line \(x+y=c\) belongs to \(\mathcal L\), then all points of \(\mathcal P_n\) whose sum equals \(c\) are covered by that single line.  
For the maximal sum \(c=n+1\) there are \(n\) points.  
Together with the two sunny lines, at most three points of this sum can be covered (each sunny line meets the diagonal in at most one point).  
Thus \(n\le 3\), contradicting \(n\ge4\). ∎

Consequently every non‑sunny line is either horizontal (\(y=b\)) or vertical (\(x=a\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 2  
Let \(h\) be the number of horizontal lines and \(v=n-2-h\) the number of vertical lines.  
Then the set of points not lying on any of these \(h+v\) lines is a rectangular grid of size \((n-v)\times (n-h)\).

*Proof.*  
A point \((a,b)\) is missed exactly when its abscissa \(a\) is not among the chosen \(v\) vertical coordinates **and** its ordinate \(b\) is not among the chosen \(h\) horizontal coordinates.  
Hence the missed points are precisely  

\[
\{(a,b)\mid a\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus\{x\text{-coordinates of vertical lines}\},
\;b\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus\{y\text{-coordinates of horizontal lines}\}\},
\]

which is a Cartesian product of two sets of cardinalities \(n-v\) and \(n-h\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 3  
The two sunny lines can cover at most \(2\) points in each missed column (or row).

*Proof.*  
A sunny line is never vertical; therefore it meets a given column \(x=\alpha\) in at most one point.  
With two sunny lines we obtain at most two points per column. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
From Lemma 2 and Lemma 3 we obtain the inequality  

\[
(n-v)(n-h)\le 2n .
\tag{2}
\]

Because \(h+v=n-2\), write \(v=n-2-h\) and substitute into (2):

\[
(h+2)(n-h)\le 2n .
\]

The left‑hand side is a quadratic concave function of \(h\) whose maximum on the interval \(0\le h\le n-2\) is attained at the endpoints; there we have equality \((h+2)(n-h)=2n\).  
Hence (2) forces  

\[
\{h,v\}=\{0,n-2\},
\]

i.e. **all** non‑sunny lines are parallel to the same axis.  
Assume without loss of generality that they are vertical; then the missed points lie in the two rightmost columns  

\[
x=n-1,\qquad x=n .
\]

For \(n\ge4\) these columns contain respectively \(2\) and \(1\) points, altogether three points:
\[
(n-1,1),\;(n-1,2),\;(n,1).
\]

A sunny line cannot contain two points with the same abscissa (that would be a vertical line), so each of the three points needs a distinct sunny line.  
Thus at least three sunny lines are necessary, contradicting the hypothesis \(k=2\). ∎

Therefore **\(k=2\) is impossible for every \(n\ge4\).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Constructions for all admissible \(k\)

Let \(t\) be an integer with \(0\le t\le n\) and \(t\neq 2\) when \(n\ge4\).  
We shall exhibit \(n\) distinct lines covering \(\mathcal P_n\) and containing exactly \(t\) sunny lines.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.1  Non‑sunny part

Take the vertical lines  

\[
x=1,\;x=2,\dots ,x=n-t .
\tag{3}
\]

If \(t=n\) this list is empty.  
These \(n-t\) lines cover every point of \(\mathcal P_n\) whose abscissa does not belong to  

\[
C_t=\{\,n-t+1,\;n-t+2,\dots ,n\,\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.2  The uncovered triangle

The points whose abscissa lies in \(C_t\) form the lattice triangle  

\[
T_t=\bigl\{(x,y)\in\mathcal P_n\mid x\in C_t\bigr\}
      =\{(n-t+j,\;j+s)\mid 1\le j\le t,\;0\le s\le t-j\}.
\tag{4}
\]

Its size is \(|T_t|=t(t+1)/2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.3  Sunny covering of \(T_t\)

For each \(j=1,2,\dots ,t\) define the line  

\[
L_j:\; y-x = j-(n-t+1) .
\tag{5}
\]

All \(L_j\) have slope \(1\); consequently they are sunny and pairwise distinct.

From (4) we see that the point \((n-t+j,\;j)\) belongs to \(L_j\).  
Because the slope is \(1\),

\[
L_j\cap T_t=\{(n-t+j+s,\;j+s)\mid 0\le s\le t-j\},
\]

i.e. \(L_j\) contains exactly the points of the \(j\)-th diagonal of the triangle \(T_t\).  
When \(j\) runs from \(1\) to \(t\) these diagonals partition \(T_t\); therefore  

\[
T_t=\bigcup_{j=1}^{t} L_j .
\tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.4  The whole family

The family  

\[
\mathcal L_t=\bigl\{\,x=i\mid 1\le i\le n-t\,\bigr\}\;\cup\;
            \bigl\{\,L_j\mid 1\le j\le t\,\bigr\}
\]

contains exactly \(n-t+t=n\) distinct lines, exactly \(t\) of which are sunny, and by (3)–(6) it covers every point of \(\mathcal P_n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.5  Special cases

* **\(t=0\).**  The construction gives the \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\).  
  Replacing the line \(x=n\) by the diagonal \(x+y=n+1\) (which is non‑sunny) yields a family with no sunny line.

* **\(t=1\).**  We have the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\) and the single sunny line \(L_1\) of slope \(1\); this covers all points.

* **\(t=n\).**  No vertical line is used; the \(n\) sunny lines are precisely \(L_1,\dots ,L_n\).  
  Their union is the whole set \(\mathcal P_n\).

* **\(n=3,\;t=2\).**  The general construction fails because the triangle \(T_2\) cannot be covered by two slope‑\(1\) lines.  
  An explicit example works:

  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  &\text{sunny lines: } y=x,\qquad y=2x-1,\\
  &\text{non‑sunny lines: } x=1,\qquad y=1 .
  \end{aligned}
  \]

  One checks directly that every point of \(\mathcal P_3\) lies on at least one of these four lines.

Thus for every \(n\ge3\) and every admissible \(k\) we have exhibited a concrete configuration.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Conclusion

* For \(n=3\) the admissible values are \(k=0,1,2,3\).  
* For every \(n\ge4\) the admissible values are all integers \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n\) **except** \(k=2\).

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\begin{cases}
\{0,1,2,3\}, & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,3,4,\dots ,n\}, & n\ge4 .
\end{cases}}
\]
